mediaItem.keyStats:
-   Tens of thousands of people incarcerated in the U.S. have been wrongfully convicted.
-   James Soto and David Ayala served 42 years in prison, the longest wrongful conviction sentences in Illinois history until their exoneration in December 2023.
-   Robert Elmodovar was wrongfully convicted and exonerated after serving over 20 years.
-   Illinois has effectively had no parole program since 1978.
mediaItem.itemTitle: Lauren Bright Pacheco with James Soto
mediaItem.summaryNotes: This episode of Wrongful Conviction features James Soto and Robert Elmodovar, two men wrongfully convicted in Chicago. James Soto recounts his arrest and conviction for a double murder in 1981, despite being 30 miles away at the time of the crime and lacking physical evidence. He served 42 years before exoneration. Robert Elmodovar, also wrongfully convicted, became cellmates with Soto in prison. The episode explores the flawed evidence in Soto's case, including coerced witness statements and lack of physical evidence.  It highlights the devastating impact of wrongful convictions, the importance of prisoner advocacy, and the enduring friendship forged between Soto and Elmodovar during their incarceration.  Both men now advocate for criminal justice reform.

keyQuotesRaw: James Soto: "I looked at the judge. I looked at the jury. Looked them in the eye. And I'm like, how could this happen? How could you come up with a guilty verdict based on such whimsy evidence?" (After guilty verdict)

James Soto: "Prisoners in the eighties and early nineties was in Illinois were particularly violent. Stable was very violent. I mean, murders occurring there. There was a lot of things that, you know, a lot of stab means a lot of assaults." (Describing prison conditions)

Robert Elmodovar on James Soto: "Jimmy Soto, I heard of him. His name is like a legend in prison basically because everybody knows who he was. Everybody knows all the work he did and how he helped a lot of people." (Describing Soto's reputation as a jailhouse lawyer)
Robert Elmodovar on their cellmate relationship: "He probably know me better than my own family to be honest with you." (Describing the depth of their bond)

James Soto on Robert Elmodovar: "He was very helpful in telling me the things I need to do... He helped me and dad any and I thank him. I thank god to have him there to be able to tell me you know some of these things and how to navigate them myself." (Describing Robert's help after Soto's exoneration)
flawed_eyewitness_testimony: Highlighted in both Soto and Elmodovar's cases.
coerced_confessions_witness_statements: Implied in Soto's case with young witnesses and explicitly mentioned regarding Detective Guavera in Elmodovar's case.
ineffective_trial_defense: Suggested by Soto's initial confidence in his lawyer despite the guilty verdict and the mention of things his attorney "didn't do."
police_misconduct_tunnel_vision: CPD's focus on gang affiliation and overlooking initial eyewitness accounts in Soto's case.  Detective Guavera's pattern of misconduct in Elmodovar's case.
impact_of_pre-trial_detention: Stress on Soto's girlfriend leading to miscarriage, loss of personal property.
brutal_prison_conditions: Violence, overcrowding, lack of resources in Illinois prisons in the 80s and 90s.
lack_of_parole_in_illinois: Mentioned as a factor in Soto's life sentence and advocacy for its reinstatement.
policyRecommendationsRaw: Donate to James Soto's GoFundMe to support his law school education and fight for justice.
Support Parole Illinois in their fight to bring back parole to Illinois.
james_soto: Lost 42 years of his life, missed family milestones, endured brutal prison conditions, but dedicated himself to legal study and helping others.  Now pursuing law degree and advocating for parole reform.  Expressed fury and disbelief at the guilty verdict and the impact on his family.
robert_elmodovar: Lost over 20 years, forged a deep bond with James Soto in prison, now actively supports other wrongfully convicted individuals and helped connect Soto with legal assistance.  Experienced the shock and disbelief of exoneration after decades of imprisonment.
